how_merit_retention_works: Florida Supreme Court justices and district court of appeal judges are appointed by the governor from nominees submitted by a judicial nominating commission and then face voters in a yes-or-no 'merit retention' question ('Shall Justice/Judge ___ be retained in office?') at the first general election held more than one year after appointment and every six years thereafter. A simple majority of votes cast on the question retains the judge for a new six-year term; a majority 'no' vote creates a vacancy that the governor fills by appointment (Fla. Const. art. V, s. 10).
ballot_context: Every Florida ballot asks whether Supreme Court Justice Carlos G. Muñiz should be retained. Voters also answer a retention question for each District Court of Appeal judge standing in their district; which judges appear depends on the county (enter your address above to see yours). Names are verified against The Florida Bar's 2026 merit-retention list and county sample ballots. The Florida Bar discontinued its merit-retention poll in 2023, so there is no 2026 Bar poll.
research_note: Third pass (Sept 17, 2026): the sample ballot and The Florida Bar's merit-retention page were fetched directly; the earlier question of a possible fourth Fifth DCA judge is resolved (there are three). Biographies were checked against the Governor's 2019 appointment release (Muñiz), Wikipedia (Makar) and Ballotpedia/Space Coast Daily/Law360 search results (Harris, Wallis); the court's own judge pages did not render in this environment.

judges.name: Carlos G. Muñiz
judges.ballot_question: Shall Justice Carlos G. Muñiz of the Supreme Court be retained in office?
judges.background: Born June 25, 1969, in Chicago. B.A. with high honors, University of Virginia (1991); J.D., Yale Law School (1997), where he was an editor of the Yale Law Journal. Law clerk to U.S. District Judge Thomas A. Flannery (D.C.) and Judge José A. Cabranes (U.S. Court of Appeals, 2nd Circuit). Deputy general counsel to Gov. Jeb Bush (2001), general counsel of the Department of Financial Services, deputy chief of staff and counsel to House Speaker Marco Rubio, deputy attorney general and chief of staff to Attorney General Pam Bondi (2011-2014), and general counsel of the U.S. Department of Education (2018-2019). Appointed to the Florida Supreme Court Jan. 22, 2019, as its 89th justice and the first Nicaraguan-American justice; retained by voters in 2020; served as the 57th Chief Justice of Florida from July 2022 to June 2026.

notable.item: Joined the court's 6-1 majority opinion (written by Justice Jamie Grosshans) in Planned Parenthood of Southwest and Central Florida v. State (April 1, 2024), holding that the Florida Constitution's privacy clause does not protect abortion and upholding the state's 15-week abortion law (which allowed the six-week law to take effect). An earlier version of this entry said he authored the opinion; sources identify Grosshans as the author.
Only Florida Supreme Court justice on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot; this is his second retention election (first retained in 2020).
Florida Channel produced an 'On the Ballot' profile segment on Justice Muñiz for the 2026 retention election.

rulings.case: Planned Parenthood of Southwest and Central Florida v. State (15-week abortion law)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court held that the privacy clause of the Florida Constitution does not protect a right to abortion, receding from its 1989 decision In re T.W. and later cases, and upheld the state's 15-week abortion law. Because the 2023 six-week law was written to take effect 30 days after such a ruling, the decision allowed the six-week law to take effect on May 1, 2024.
rulings.note: The majority opinion was written by Justice Jamie Grosshans and joined by Justices Muñiz, Canady, Couriel and Francis; Justice Sasso concurred separately on standing; Justice Labarga dissented. (The earlier claim in this file that Muñiz authored the majority was not supported by sources.)

rulings.case: Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re: Limiting Government Interference with Abortion (Amendment 4 ballot placement)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court approved the citizen-initiated abortion-rights amendment (Amendment 4) for the November 2024 ballot, finding that it addressed a single subject and that its ballot summary was not misleading. In November 2024 the measure fell short of the 60% approval needed to pass.
rulings.note: Muñiz was in the four-justice majority and wrote a separate opinion saying the initiative was an appropriate matter to put before voters; Justice Grosshans dissented (joined by Justice Sasso) saying the summary 'misleads by omission,' and Justice Sasso wrote a dissent joined by Justices Grosshans and Francis. The author of the majority opinion (reported as the court's opinion) was not identified in available sources.

rulings.case: State v. Poole
rulings.what_it_decided: The court receded in part from its 2016 Hurst v. State decision, holding that the Florida and U.S. constitutions do not require a unanimous jury recommendation before a judge may impose a death sentence; it reinstated a death sentence that an 11-1 jury had recommended. The ruling did not itself change the 2017 statute that then required a unanimous recommendation.
rulings.note: The opinion was unsigned (per curiam); the court had five sitting members at the time. Justice Labarga dissented, writing that the decision returned Florida to 'absolute outlier' status among death-penalty states.

rulings.case: Advisory Opinion to the Governor re: Implementation of Amendment 4, the Voting Restoration Amendment
rulings.what_it_decided: In a non-binding advisory opinion requested by Gov. DeSantis, the court concluded that the phrase 'all terms of sentence' in the 2018 felon-voting amendment includes legal financial obligations such as fines, fees and restitution, so a person with a felony conviction must pay those before regaining the right to vote.
rulings.vote: Majority of Canady, Polston, Lawson and Muñiz; Labarga wrote separately (reported as 4-1 by Florida Politics, as unanimous on the core holding by Florida Phoenix)
rulings.note: The court had five members at the time. Justice Labarga agreed with the result in part but wrote separately, objecting to the majority's strictly textual approach and a point about informing voters.

rulings.case: In re Amendments to the Florida Evidence Code (adoption of the Daubert standard)
rulings.what_it_decided: Using its rulemaking power, the court adopted the Legislature's 2013 'Daubert' amendments governing when expert testimony is admissible, replacing the older 'Frye' general-acceptance test and reversing the court's own 2017 and 2018 decisions that had kept Frye. The change affects how judges screen expert witnesses in civil and criminal trials.
rulings.note: The decision was per curiam; Muñiz also joined Justice Lawson's concurrence responding to Justice Luck's procedural dissent. Justices Labarga and Luck dissented separately.

rulings.case: Advisory Opinion to the Attorney General re: Prohibits Possession of Defined Assault Weapons (assault-weapons ban initiative)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court removed a proposed constitutional amendment banning 'assault weapons' from consideration for the ballot, finding the ballot summary misleading because it told voters existing weapons would be exempted and registered when the text exempted only the current owner's possession. The court reviewed only the ballot wording, not the merits of a ban; sponsors would have had to restart the petition process.
rulings.note: Chief Justice Canady and Justices Polston, Lawson and Muñiz formed the majority; Justice Labarga dissented.

rulings.case: Black Voters Matter Capacity Building Institute v. Byrd (2022 congressional map)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court upheld the 2022 congressional map that dismantled a North Florida district in which Black voters had been able to elect their candidate of choice. It held that the challengers had not shown a district could be drawn that satisfied the state constitution's 'non-diminishment' rule without race predominating in violation of the federal Equal Protection Clause, and that lawmakers' federal obligation took precedence.
rulings.note: Justice Labarga dissented, writing that the decision left in place a plan that is unconstitutional under the Florida Constitution and should have been returned to the trial court.

rulings.case: Equal Ground Education Fund v. State (request to block the 2026 congressional map)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court declined to take up a request by Equal Ground Education Fund to intervene in, or use its 'all writs' power to bypass, a pending First District Court of Appeal case over a trial court's refusal to block the Legislature's 2026 congressional map, saying it lacked jurisdiction at that stage. The practical effect was that the new map governed the 2026 congressional elections.
rulings.note: Justice Labarga was the lone dissenter, arguing the constitution anticipates expedited review of urgent statewide matters. The opinion's author was not identified in available reports (one outlet attributes a quoted statement to Justice Adam Tanenbaum); Muñiz's membership in the majority is inferred from the 6-1 vote with Labarga as the only dissenter.

rulings.case: Prentice v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. (Engle-progeny smoker lawsuits)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court held that smokers (or their survivors) suing tobacco companies for fraudulent concealment or conspiracy in 'Engle progeny' cases must prove they relied on specific statements or omissions by the companies, rather than letting juries infer reliance generally. The ruling made it harder for plaintiffs in the thousands of remaining Florida tobacco cases to win fraud claims.
rulings.note: Justice Labarga dissented, writing that settled Florida law had allowed juries to infer reliance. Muñiz's authorship is reported by Florida Bulldog; the Justia docket (SC20-943) carries the opinion.

rulings.case: In re Amendments to Rules Regulating The Florida Bar (continuing-legal-education diversity policy)
rulings.what_it_decided: Acting on its own motion, the court amended Bar rules so that Florida lawyers cannot receive continuing-legal-education credit for programs that require panels to meet diversity quotas, a response to a policy adopted by the Bar's Business Law Section modeled on an American Bar Association guideline. chief_justice_tenure.summary: Muñiz was elected chief justice unanimously by his colleagues in 2022 (term beginning July 1, 2022) and re-elected to a second two-year term in 2024; Wikipedia lists John D. Couriel as his successor as of July 1, 2026. As chief justice he was the judicial branch's chief administrator and spokesperson to the Legislature on budget and policy.

items.item: Oversaw a rewrite of Florida's civil procedure rules, effective Jan. 1, 2025, that requires early case-management orders, firmer deadlines and changes to discovery; Florida Bar News describes it as the most significant overhaul of the state's civil justice system in over half a century. Muñiz has called the reforms a work in progress and said the court will keep studying unintended consequences.

Led the court's legislative budget requests for case-management technology, court reporters and interpreters, and judgeships; the court certified a need for 50 additional judgeships in a December order and the Legislature approved 39 new trial and appellate judgeships in 2025. He has briefed House panels on court efficiency reforms.
Elected chief justice by unanimous vote of the court in 2022, succeeding Charles Canady, and re-elected in 2024 for a second term beginning July 1, 2024.

judges.record_summary: Observers across the spectrum describe Muñiz as a reliable member of the court's majority: Florida Bulldog, which has been critical of the court, characterizes the DeSantis-era court as 'conservative' and notes its decisions tend to be unanimous or 6-1 with Justice Jorge Labarga as the usual dissenter, while the Florida Phoenix's 2026 voter guide notes that his 2019 appointment was praised by John Stemberger of the Florida Family Policy Council, an anti-abortion group, and points voters to his votes upholding the 15-week abortion law, allowing the 2024 abortion and marijuana amendments onto the ballot, and upholding the congressional map that eliminated a majority-Black North Florida district. The Florida Trib reported in October 2026 that the Miami Herald editorial board urged voters not to retain him while the Sun Sentinel editorial board said he deserves retention. The Florida Bar's last merit-retention polls (2020) found 71% of responding lawyers favored retaining him. As of late October 2026, no organized 'vote no' or 'vote yes' committee, campaign spending, or formal position from Planned Parenthood, the Florida Democratic Party, Florida Rising, or the League of Women Voters on his retention was found in searches; Ballotpedia and news outlets note that no Florida Supreme Court justice has ever lost a retention vote.
